title: How to choose a home care agency in New Jersey
dek: What New Jersey law requires of home care companies, how to check a license in minutes, what care costs and who pays, and the questions that separate a good agency from a risky one.
keyFacts: Home care firms must register with the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs
Aides giving hands-on care through an agency must be certified CHHAs
CareScout 2025: NJ non-medical home care about $86,944 a year at 44 hours a week
Medicare does not pay for custodial care when it is the only care needed
Free screening for public programs: ADRC 1-877-222-3737
body:
Bringing a stranger into a parent's home is a big step. The right aide can mean Mom keeps living in the house she loves. The wrong one can mean missed shifts, a sloppy bath or worse. The difference often comes down to a few checks most families skip.

This guide explains what New Jersey law requires of home care companies, how to look up a license in a few minutes, what care costs here, who pays for what, and the questions and warning signs that matter most.

What kind of help does your parent need?

Start here, because the answer decides what kind of company you call. Home care falls into three broad levels.

  • Companion and homemaker help. Company, light housekeeping, meals, errands, reminders and rides. No hands-on body care.
  • Personal care. Hands-on help with bathing, dressing, toileting, moving from bed to chair and eating. In New Jersey, an agency that sends someone to do this work must send a Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aide (CHHA).
  • Skilled care. Nursing and therapy ordered by a doctor, such as wound care, injections, or physical, occupational and speech therapy. This comes from a licensed home health agency, often after a hospital stay.

Many families need a mix. A father recovering from a hip replacement might get skilled therapy visits from a home health agency and a few hours a day of personal care from a separate home care company. Write down the tasks, the hours and the days before you start calling. Agencies quote faster and more honestly when you can be specific.

What licenses should a New Jersey home care company have?

New Jersey regulates home care more tightly than many states. There are three things to check.

Health care service firm registration

Most private-pay home care companies are what state law calls a health care service firm. The NJ Division of Consumer Affairs defines this as an agency that places or arranges for the placement of people who provide health or personal care in clients' homes. Every such firm must register with the Division and renew. Firms are also required to be accredited by an approved accrediting body, and the Division posts the list of approved accreditors on its health care service firm page.

Home health agency license

Agencies that send nurses and therapists for skilled care, and bill Medicare for it, are licensed by the NJ Department of Health. Your parent's doctor or hospital discharge planner will usually arrange this kind of agency.

CHHA certification for the aide

The aide is licensed separately from the company. Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aides are certified by the New Jersey Board of Nursing. The Division of Consumer Affairs has warned that a firm must verify an aide's certification before placing that aide, and may only send a certified aide to a client who needs CHHA services. Firms have faced penalties for sending uncertified workers.

  1. Look up the company. Use the Division of Consumer Affairs License Verification System. Choose a business search and check that the firm's registration is active.
  2. Look up the aide. Ask for the aide's full name and certification number before the first shift, then run a person search in the same system.
  3. Ask about complaints. Call the Division's Regulated Businesses Section at 973-504-6370 with questions about a firm's registration.
  4. Ask for accreditation. Ask which body accredited the firm and when. A good agency answers right away.
Check the company and the aide. They are licensed separately.

Agency, registry or private hire: which is right?

There are three common ways to find an aide. Each trades cost against protection and convenience.

OptionWho is the employer?What to know
Home care agencyThe agencyIt screens, trains, supervises, pays payroll taxes and finds a fill-in when an aide is sick. You pay more per hour for that.
Registry or referral serviceVaries, so askIt matches you with an aide, and in some setups your family becomes the employer. Ask whether it is registered with Consumer Affairs and who handles taxes, insurance and backup.
Private hireYour familyOften cheaper per hour, and you choose the person. You also handle background checks, payroll, taxes, insurance and coverage when the aide is out.

If you hire privately, you may be a household employer. The IRS explains the rules in Publication 926, Household Employer's Tax Guide. Talk with an accountant, and ask your insurance agent whether your parent's policy covers an injury to a household worker. Families sometimes start with private hire to save money and switch to an agency after the first missed weekend.

How much does home care cost in New Jersey?

Rates vary by county, by agency and by the hours you need. Nights, weekends, holidays and short shifts often cost more. For a benchmark, CareScout (the long-term care company connected with Genworth) publishes an annual Cost of Care survey. Its 2025 figures for New Jersey, released in March 2026, include:

Type of care (NJ, 2025)Annual cost
Home care, non-medical caregiver (44 hours a week)$86,944
Adult day health care (5 days a week)$26,000
Assisted living, private one-bedroom$101,550
Nursing home, semi-private room$153,300

The home care figure works out to roughly $38 an hour. Treat it as a reference point. Your quotes may be higher or lower. Ask every agency for its hourly rate in writing, along with any minimum shift length and the rate for live-in care.

Will Medicare or NJ FamilyCare pay for it?

This is where many families get a surprise.

Medicare

Medicare covers home health care only when your parent is homebound, needs part-time or intermittent skilled nursing or therapy, and a doctor orders it. A Medicare-certified agency must provide it. In that case Medicare can also pay for some aide visits while the skilled care continues. Medicare does not cover 24-hour care at home, meal delivery, homemaker services, or personal care such as bathing and dressing when that is the only help your parent needs. Most ongoing aide care is paid privately.

NJ FamilyCare and MLTSS

New Jersey's Medicaid program, NJ FamilyCare, can pay for Personal Care Assistant (PCA) services for members who qualify. Members who need a nursing home level of care may enroll in Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS), which adds services such as respite, care management, home modifications, meals and an emergency response system. Read our guide to Medicaid and MLTSS for the income and asset rules.

Members approved for PCA services may be able to use the Personal Preference Program, which lets them hire their own workers, including friends, relatives or neighbors, instead of using an agency. The state PPP office is at 609-631-2481.

Other ways to pay

  • Long-term care insurance. Find the policy, check the elimination period and ask whether the agency will bill the insurer.
  • State programs for people who do not qualify for Medicaid. The Statewide Respite Care Program and Jersey Assistance for Community Caregiving (JACC) can help pay for aides. See our caregiver respite guide.
  • Veterans benefits. Veterans and surviving spouses may qualify for help through the VA. Ask a county veterans service officer.
Start with one free call

The Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) at 1-877-222-3737 connects you to your county office on aging. Staff can screen your parent for public programs before you commit to private pay.

What should I ask before signing with an agency?

Interview at least two or three agencies. Take notes, and notice who answers clearly and who gets vague.

  • Are you registered with the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs, and who accredits you?
  • Are your aides employees of the agency, or independent contractors?
  • Are all aides who give hands-on care certified CHHAs?
  • What background checks do you run, and how often do you repeat them?
  • Is a registered nurse involved in the care plan? How often does a supervisor visit?
  • What happens if the aide calls out sick? How much notice will we get?
  • Can we meet the aide first, and can we ask for a different aide?
  • What is the hourly rate, the minimum shift, and the rate for nights, weekends and holidays?
  • Do you carry liability insurance and workers' compensation coverage?
  • How do we cancel, and how much notice do you need?
  • Do aides help with medications, or only give reminders?

Read the service agreement before you sign. Look for the cancellation terms, deposit rules, billing cycle and how rate increases are handled.

What are the red flags?

  • The company cannot show an active registration, or will not tell you who accredits it.
  • They send someone for bathing or toileting who is not a certified CHHA.
  • They ask for large payments in cash, or months of fees up front.
  • They pressure you to sign the same day.
  • No one from the office visits to assess your parent before care starts.
  • Aides change constantly and no one explains why.
  • Your parent seems afraid of an aide, or money, jewelry or medications go missing.

If something feels wrong, act quickly. Call the agency supervisor. You can file a complaint with the Division of Consumer Affairs. If you suspect abuse, neglect or exploitation, contact Adult Protective Services in your county through the ADRC, or call 911 in an emergency. Our guide to scams in New Jersey covers financial red flags too.

Can a geriatric care manager help?

Yes, especially if you live far away or the situation is complicated. A geriatric care manager, usually a social worker or nurse, can assess your parent, recommend the right level of care, screen agencies, and keep an eye on how the aide is doing. Most charge by the hour, and Medicare does not pay for it. Read our guide on when to call a geriatric care manager.

If you have not yet talked with your parent about getting help, our guide to the first conversation about care can help. For ideas on making the house itself safer, see aging in place in New Jersey.

faq.q: How do I check if a home care agency is licensed in New Jersey?
faq.a: Use the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs License Verification System at newjersey.mylicense.com and search for the business. Home care companies that place aides are registered as health care service firms. You can also call the Division's Regulated Businesses Section at 973-504-6370.

faq.q: What is a CHHA in New Jersey?
faq.a: A CHHA is a Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aide, certified by the New Jersey Board of Nursing. Agencies must send a certified CHHA when a client needs hands-on personal care such as bathing or toileting.

faq.q: How much does a home health aide cost per hour in New Jersey?
faq.a: CareScout's 2025 Cost of Care survey put New Jersey non-medical home care at $86,944 a year for 44 hours a week, which works out to roughly $38 an hour. Actual rates vary by county, agency and schedule, so get written quotes.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for a home health aide?
faq.a: Only as part of Medicare home health care, when your parent is homebound and also needs skilled nursing or therapy ordered by a doctor. Medicare does not pay for ongoing help with bathing, dressing or housekeeping when that is the only care needed.

faq.q: Does NJ Medicaid pay family members to be caregivers?
faq.a: NJ FamilyCare members approved for Personal Care Assistant services may be able to join the Personal Preference Program and hire their own workers, including relatives. Call the member's health plan or the state PPP office at 609-631-2481.

NJ Division of Medical Assistance and Health Services: MLTSS
NJ Division of Medical Assistance and Health Services: Personal Preference Program

title: When a parent leaves the hospital: a New Jersey family guide
dek: Observation versus inpatient, the 3-day rule for rehab coverage, how to appeal a discharge, and a checklist for the day your parent comes home.
keyFacts: Observation days do not count toward Medicare's 3-day inpatient rule for nursing facility rehab
MOON notice: due within 36 hours for people under observation more than 24 hours
2026 SNF coinsurance: $0 for days 1 to 20, $217 a day for days 21 to 100
Appeal a discharge through Livanta (Commence Health): 1-866-815-5440
body:
The call often comes on a weekday morning. "Your mother is being discharged today." Suddenly you have a few hours to sort out rides, prescriptions, equipment and who will be with her tonight. Many families feel rushed, and some get stuck with bills they did not see coming.

You have more say than you may think. This guide walks through discharge planning, the difference between inpatient and observation status, the rules for Medicare coverage of rehab, how to appeal a discharge, and what to do on the day itself and the week after. Figures are for Original Medicare in 2026. Medicare Advantage plans have their own rules, so call the plan too.

When does discharge planning start?

Earlier than most families realize. Hospitals are supposed to start planning soon after admission. Every hospital has discharge planners, usually nurses or social workers, sometimes called case managers.

Ask for the planner's name and direct number on the first or second day. Tell them who the main family contact is and what the home situation looks like. Be honest. If Dad lives alone in a split-level in Cherry Hill and you live in Ohio, the planner needs to know that now, not at 10 a.m. on discharge day.

If your parent is able, have them tell staff that you may receive information about their care. Bring a copy of any health care power of attorney or advance directive. Our estate planning guide explains those documents.

Is my parent an inpatient or under observation?

This is the most important question you can ask, and you should ask it in those words. A person can spend nights in a hospital bed without being admitted. They may be an outpatient receiving observation services.

Why it matters:

  • Inpatient care is billed under Medicare Part A. Observation is billed under Part B, with different costs.
  • Days under observation do not count toward the 3-day inpatient stay that Medicare requires before it covers a skilled nursing facility.

The MOON notice

Hospitals must give a Medicare patient who has been under observation for more than 24 hours a written notice called the Medicare Outpatient Observation Notice (MOON). It must be delivered no later than 36 hours after observation begins, or sooner if the patient is released first. It explains that your parent is an outpatient and how that affects costs and nursing facility coverage. A MOON is a notice and cannot be appealed. It is your signal to ask questions.

If status changes from inpatient to observation

Sometimes a hospital admits someone, then changes them to observation. Since February 14, 2025, people with Original Medicare have a right to a fast appeal of that change. The hospital should give you a Medicare Change of Status Notice (form CMS-10868) before your parent leaves. If you do not get one, ask for it. The appeal goes to the Beneficiary and Family Centered Care Quality Improvement Organization (BFCC-QIO), and Medicare.gov says a decision usually comes about 2 days after you file. Medicare explains the process here.

Ask in plain words: is she admitted as an inpatient, or here under observation?

Will Medicare pay for rehab in a nursing facility?

Original Medicare Part A covers short-term care in a skilled nursing facility (SNF) only when several conditions are met:

  • Your parent had a medically necessary inpatient stay of at least 3 days in a row. The day of discharge does not count. Observation and emergency room time do not count either.
  • They enter a Medicare-certified SNF, generally within 30 days of leaving the hospital.
  • They need daily skilled nursing or therapy for a condition treated in the hospital.
SNF stay, per benefit period (2026)What your parent pays
Days 1 to 20$0 per day (after the Part A deductible of $1,736, if not already paid)
Days 21 to 100$217 per day
Day 101 and beyondAll costs

There are exceptions. Some Medicare Advantage plans waive the 3-day rule. So do some doctors who are part of an Accountable Care Organization with an approved waiver. Ask the planner whether either applies. A Medigap plan may cover the daily coinsurance for days 21 to 100. See our Medicare Advantage vs. Medigap guide.

How do I appeal a discharge that feels too soon?

If your parent was admitted as an inpatient, the hospital must give them a notice called An Important Message from Medicare about Your Rights. It comes within 2 days of admission, and usually again no more than 2 days before discharge. Read it. It lists the phone number for the appeal.

New Jersey's BFCC-QIO is the organization Medicare has long contracted as Livanta, which CMS now lists under the name Commence Health. The Region 2 helpline for New Jersey and New York is 1-866-815-5440.

  1. Call before your parent leaves. Request the review no later than the day of discharge. A phone call is enough to start it.
  2. Say why. For example: she cannot yet walk to the bathroom, the wound is not healing, or no safe plan exists at home.
  3. Stay put while it is reviewed. If you file on time, the hospital generally cannot bill your parent for the extra time while the QIO decides, apart from usual deductibles and coinsurance.
  4. Expect a quick answer. The QIO usually decides within about a day of getting the medical records.

Medicare Advantage members have the same right to a QIO review of a hospital discharge. For free, unbiased help with any Medicare appeal, call New Jersey's State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) at 1-800-792-8820.

What are the options after the hospital?

  • Home with home health care. If your parent is homebound and needs skilled nursing or therapy, Medicare covers part-time visits from a certified home health agency at no cost for covered services. It does not cover round-the-clock aides.
  • Skilled nursing facility. Short-term rehab in a nursing home, under the rules above.
  • Inpatient rehabilitation facility. For people who need intensive therapy and close medical supervision, often after a stroke, major surgery or a serious injury. A doctor must certify the need.
  • Home with outpatient therapy. For people who can travel to appointments.
  • Home with private help. Many families add paid aides for the first weeks. Our guide to choosing a home care agency explains what to check.

You have the right to choose among facilities and agencies. Ask the planner for a list, check quality ratings on Medicare's Care Compare tool, and call the places yourself. Ask whether they have a bed or opening, and whether they take your parent's insurance.

What if the plan for home does not look safe?

Speak up early, and in writing if you can. Discharge planners work with what they are told. If no one mentions that the only bathroom is upstairs, the plan may assume your parent can climb stairs.

Ask for a short family meeting with the planner, a nurse and, if possible, the physical therapist. Questions worth asking:

  • Can she safely get to the bathroom, in and out of bed, and up the front steps? Has therapy actually tested that?
  • How many hours of help a day will she need for the first two weeks?
  • What happens if the home health agency cannot start visits for several days?
  • Would a short rehab stay be safer, and does she qualify for Medicare coverage of one?

Say you live in Bergen County and your father lives alone in Toms River. Tell the planner plainly that no one can stay with him at night. That fact changes the safe options, and the planner should record it. If you still believe the discharge is unsafe, use the appeal steps above before he leaves.

A checklist for the day of discharge

  • Get the written discharge instructions and go over them with the nurse, out loud, before you leave.
  • Ask: what is the diagnosis, what should we watch for, and who do we call at 2 a.m.?
  • Get a full, updated medication list (more on that below).
  • Confirm that new prescriptions have been sent to a pharmacy that is open, and that it has them in stock.
  • Confirm the delivery date for any equipment, such as a walker, commode, hospital bed or oxygen.
  • Get the name and number of the home health agency or rehab facility, and the date of the first visit.
  • Arrange the ride. Bring warm clothes, shoes that fit over swollen feet, and a pillow for the car.
  • Make sure someone will be at home for at least the first night.
  • Stock easy food and fill the first prescriptions on the way home.

Why does medication reconciliation matter?

Medication mix-ups are a common reason people end up back in the hospital. Hospitals often stop, start or change doses. The pills in the kitchen cabinet may not match the new plan.

Before you leave, ask for a list showing every medicine, the dose and when to take it. Ask which home medicines to stop. When you get home, gather every bottle, including vitamins and over-the-counter products, and compare them with the list. Bring the list and the bottles to the first doctor visit. Ask the pharmacist to look for duplicates and interactions. If cost is a barrier, see our guide to prescription and bill help in New Jersey.

Why book a follow-up visit within 7 days?

The first week home is the riskiest. A visit with the primary care doctor within about 7 days gives someone a chance to check the medication list, review test results, catch early warning signs and adjust the plan. Book the appointment before you leave the hospital if you can. If your parent cannot get to the office, ask about a home visit or telehealth.

Ask the hospital which symptoms mean you should call the doctor and which mean you should call 911. Write them on the refrigerator.

Need help arranging care at home?

Call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 to reach your county office on aging. A geriatric care manager can also step in quickly when you live far away.

faq.q: What is the difference between inpatient and observation status?
faq.a: An inpatient has been formally admitted on a doctor's order, and the stay is billed under Medicare Part A. A patient under observation is an outpatient billed under Part B, even after overnight stays, and those days do not count toward the 3-day stay Medicare requires for skilled nursing facility coverage.

faq.q: Does Medicare still require a 3-day hospital stay for rehab in a nursing home?
faq.a: Yes, for Original Medicare. Your parent needs a medically necessary inpatient stay of at least 3 days in a row, not counting the day of discharge. Some Medicare Advantage plans and certain Accountable Care Organizations waive the rule.

faq.q: How do I appeal a hospital discharge in New Jersey?
faq.a: Call the BFCC-QIO for New Jersey, Livanta (now operating as Commence Health), at 1-866-815-5440 no later than the day of discharge. The number is also on the Important Message from Medicare notice the hospital gives you.

The Medicare Outpatient Observation Notice tells a patient they are an outpatient under observation, not an inpatient. Hospitals must give it to people who have been under observation for more than 24 hours, no later than 36 hours after observation starts.

faq.q: How much does Medicare pay for skilled nursing facility care in 2026?
faq.a: Original Medicare pays in full for days 1 to 20 after the Part A deductible. For days 21 to 100 you pay $217 a day, and after day 100 you pay all costs.

faq.q: How soon should my parent see a doctor after leaving the hospital?
faq.a: Try to book a follow-up visit with the primary care doctor within about 7 days. Bring the discharge papers, the medication list and all pill bottles.

title: After a dementia diagnosis: where New Jersey families can turn
dek: Helplines, memory cafes, adult day and respite programs, safety steps and the legal planning to do now, for New Jersey families facing Alzheimer's or another dementia.
keyFacts: Alzheimer's New Jersey Helpline: 1-888-280-6055 (weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.)
Alzheimer's Adult Day Services Program pays 20% to 100% of adult day costs
Respite and JACC: start with the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737
Sign power of attorney and advance directive papers while your loved one still can
body:
A dementia diagnosis lands differently in every family. Some feel relief at finally having a name for what has been happening. Others feel shock, grief or fear. Most feel all of those within the same week.

What helps most is knowing that you do not have to figure this out alone. New Jersey has two strong dementia organizations, free helplines, memory cafes in libraries and town halls, state-funded adult day and respite programs, and county safety programs. This guide shows you where to start and what to do in the first months.

What should we do in the first few weeks?

You do not need to solve everything at once. Focus on a short list.

  1. Understand the diagnosis. Ask the doctor what type of dementia it is, what stage, and what to expect over the next year. Ask whether any treatments or clinical trials might fit.
  2. Make one call for support. Call one of the helplines below. A trained person can listen and point you to local help.
  3. Get the legal papers done while your loved one can still take part. More on this below.
  4. Look at safety. Driving, medications, the stove and wandering are the big four.
  5. Tell the people who need to know. Close family, a trusted neighbor and, if your loved one is comfortable, friends from church or the senior center.

If the person with the diagnosis is your parent, include them in decisions as much as possible. Early on, many people can say clearly what they want. Writing it down now spares the family hard guessing later.

Who can we call in New Jersey?

Two separate nonprofits serve New Jersey families, and you can use both.

OrganizationPhoneHours
Alzheimer's New Jersey (Roseland)1-888-280-6055Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Alzheimer's Association, New Jersey Chapter1-800-272-390024 hours a day, 7 days a week
Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC)1-877-222-3737Connects you to your county office on aging

Alzheimer's New Jersey is a New Jersey nonprofit based in Roseland. Its professionally staffed helpline offers confidential guidance, help with planning and referrals, with translation in many languages. It also runs family support groups, caregiver education and a respite and wellness program.

The Alzheimer's Association New Jersey Chapter is part of the national organization. You may see it called the Greater New Jersey Chapter in older materials. Its helpline answers around the clock, which matters at 3 a.m. when you are not sure what to do. The chapter lists caregiver support groups, early-stage groups for people living with the diagnosis, and free education programs.

Save both helpline numbers in your phone today, before you need them.

What is a memory cafe?

A memory cafe is a relaxed, social gathering for people living with memory loss and the people who care for them. There may be music, art, a speaker or just coffee and conversation. Nobody has to explain anything. For many couples, it is the first outing in months where they both feel at ease.

In New Jersey, public libraries and towns host many of them. Examples include the Montclair Memory Cafe (a joint effort of the township and the Montclair Public Library), the East Brunswick Public Library and the Somerset County Library System's Manville branch. Schedules change, so call ahead. To find one near you, search the Dementia Friendly America memory cafe directory, ask your library, or ask either helpline.

For other low-pressure outings, see our guide to staying connected in New Jersey.

Could an adult day program help?

Adult day programs give the person with dementia a safe, structured day with activities, meals and company. They give the caregiver regular weekday hours to work, rest or run errands. Many offer transportation.

Social adult day programs focus on activities and supervision. Adult medical day programs add nursing, therapy and help with personal care. Many centers in New Jersey have dementia-specific programs, so ask.

Alzheimer's Adult Day Services Program

The NJ Division of Aging Services runs the Alzheimer's Adult Day Services Program. It helps pay for adult day care for people with a physician-documented diagnosis of Alzheimer's or a related dementia who live in the community and have an unpaid caregiver. The subsidy covers 20% to 100% of the cost, for up to five days a week.

  • The state's posted 2025 limits were $50,256 in annual income and $40,000 in liquid assets for a single person, and $58,632 and $60,000 for a married couple. Ask for the current figures.
  • People enrolled in Medicaid, MLTSS, JACC or the Statewide Respite Care Program cannot use it at the same time.
  • You apply through a participating adult day center. The program office is at 609-438-4733.

What respite help is available?

Caring for someone with dementia is a marathon. Caregivers who take regular breaks tend to last longer. New Jersey's Statewide Respite Care Program and Jersey Assistance for Community Caregiving (JACC) can help pay for aides, adult day care and short facility stays. Both are reached through the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737. Our caregiver respite guide covers the 2026 income limits and how to apply.

If paid help at home is the answer, read our guide to choosing a home care agency in New Jersey. Ask agencies whether their aides have dementia training.

How do we keep our loved one safe?

Wandering

Many people with dementia wander or get lost at some point, even on familiar walks. Plan before it happens.

  • Keep a recent photo and a written description on hand.
  • Consider an ID bracelet with a contact phone number.
  • Ask your county sheriff's office about Project Lifesaver. Several New Jersey sheriffs, including Morris County, run this program, which uses a radio transmitter worn on the wrist to help officers find someone quickly.
  • Tell trusted neighbors so they can call you if they see your loved one out alone.

If your loved one goes missing, call 911 right away. Do not wait. New Jersey has a Silver Alert system for missing people with dementia or another cognitive impairment, and police can request one when the person is believed to be driving and in danger.

Driving

Dementia eventually makes driving unsafe, but the timing differs for every person. Ask the doctor for guidance, and consider a professional driving evaluation. Our guide to driving later in life in New Jersey covers how to have the conversation and other ways to get around.

At home

Lock up medications, firearms and car keys if needed. Consider stove shut-off devices, nightlights and removing loose rugs. Our guide to aging in place has more ideas.

Money

People with memory loss are frequent targets of scams. Watch for new "friends," unusual withdrawals and unfamiliar subscriptions. See our guide to scams in New Jersey.

What legal and financial planning should we do now?

This is the most time-sensitive step. A person must have enough capacity to sign legal documents. In early dementia, many people still can. Later, the family may need a court-appointed guardian, which takes time and money.

  • Durable power of attorney. Names someone to handle money and property.
  • Advance directive. Names a health care representative and records wishes about treatment.
  • A will, and a review of beneficiaries on bank, retirement and insurance accounts.
  • A plan for long-term care costs. Medicaid planning has strict look-back rules. An elder law attorney can explain them.

Our estate planning guide explains each document. For how Medicaid pays for long-term care, see our guide to Medicaid and MLTSS.

How do we plan for the road ahead?

Dementia usually changes slowly, over years. Needs that seem far off now, such as help with bathing or supervision through the night, tend to arrive gradually. Families who talk about the next stage early make calmer choices when it comes.

Use the doctor visits well. Bring one written page with changes you have noticed since the last appointment: sleep, mood, falls, weight, confusion at night, trouble with pills. Ask what to watch for next, and which changes mean you should call right away. Sudden new confusion can have another cause, such as an infection or a medication problem, and is worth a prompt call.

Talk, too, about where care will happen as needs grow. Some families add paid help at home. Others look at assisted living with a memory care unit, or a nursing home. Visit a few places before you need one, so a hospital stay does not force a rushed choice. Our guide to housing options in New Jersey explains the differences, and our hospital discharge guide covers what to do if a hospital stay comes first.

Here is a hypothetical example. Say your mother in Freehold was diagnosed this fall and still lives alone. A reasonable first-year plan might be a helpline call this week, legal papers signed this month, a memory cafe once a month, an adult day program two days a week by spring, and a family check-in every few months to decide what comes next.

Where can caregivers find support?

Support groups are where caregivers learn the practical tricks nobody else teaches, and where they feel understood. Both Alzheimer's New Jersey and the Alzheimer's Association list groups across the state, in person and online. Some groups are for spouses, some for adult children, and some for people living with early-stage dementia themselves.

Also look after your own health. Keep your own doctor appointments. Accept help when it is offered, and be specific when you ask for it: "Can you sit with Mom on Thursday afternoon?" works better than "Let me know if you can help." A geriatric care manager can take some of the coordination off your plate.

faq.q: Who do I call after a dementia diagnosis in New Jersey?
faq.a: Call the Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline at 1-800-272-3900 or the Alzheimer's New Jersey Helpline at 1-888-280-6055 on weekdays. For state programs, call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 to reach your county office on aging.

faq.q: What is the difference between Alzheimer's New Jersey and the Alzheimer's Association?
faq.a: Alzheimer's New Jersey is an independent New Jersey nonprofit based in Roseland. The Alzheimer's Association New Jersey Chapter is part of the national organization. Both offer helplines, support groups and education, and families can use both.

faq.q: Are there memory cafes in New Jersey?
faq.a: Yes. Libraries and towns host many, including in Montclair, East Brunswick and the Somerset County Library System's Manville branch. Search the Dementia Friendly America memory cafe directory or ask your local library.

faq.q: Does New Jersey help pay for adult day care for someone with dementia?
faq.a: Yes. The Alzheimer's Adult Day Services Program covers 20% to 100% of adult day costs for eligible people with a documented dementia diagnosis, up to five days a week. Income and asset limits apply, and you apply through a participating adult day center.

faq.q: What should I do if someone with dementia goes missing?
faq.a: Call 911 right away and give police a recent photo and description. New Jersey has a Silver Alert system, and some county sheriffs run Project Lifesaver tracking bracelets for people at risk of wandering.
